new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (Stout & Thomson 1974: intensity 'ocorre normalmente na última sílaba do tema da palavra', /pu'nu/ vs /pu'nu-řɛ/): Jefferson's underlined tonic syllables are stem-final throughout, word-final in bare words (porpot̲, akamàt̲, parkà̲) and non-final only where a postposition or enclitic follows the stem (pur̲mã, mỳ̲kam, ngri̲re = Stout & Thomson's diminutive case). It is shown by an exercise, not stated as a rule, and adds nothing on weight or secondary stress; consistent also with Salanova 2001's 'sílaba tônica (subjacentemente final)'. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar (a language-learning course, 'não se trata de uma gramática descritiva') never states a stress rule in words; its one stress exercise (Seção 2, Unidade 5, printed p. 142) marks the tonic syllable by underlining. The underlines, read off the rendered page scan (150 dpi, p. 143), put stress on the LAST syllable of every bare word or phrase-final lexical word in the left column (porpot, bàridjwa, bàygogo, djà, djwỳnh, parkà, akamàt) and, in the right column, on the last syllable of the lexical stem BEFORE a following grammatical element: postpositions mã 'para' (pur-mã 'to the garden') and kam 'em/no/na' (mỳ-kam, urkwã-kam, kàmrãnhtỳx-kam), diminutive/attenuative -re (ngri-re 'um pouquinho'; cf. Stout & Thomson's /pu'nu-řɛ/ 'mauzinho'), and -ri, -bê, -re in mrãm-ri, te-bê 'rapidamente', mak-re. I.e. stem-final stress with unstressed enclitics/postpositions, shown by example rather than stated. Elsewhere (printed pp. 80-81, 90) the book teaches that unwritten 'extra' vowels are pronounced after final consonants, chiefly r (i after ar), which matches Salanova's epenthetic echo vowel outside the stress-bearing stem syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Phrase level only: printed p. 138-139 'Na língua falada, um tom de voz alto na vogal alongada marca a ênfase, além de marcar o tempo mais longo em pronunciá-la' (emphatic vowel lengthening carries high pitch).
new_statements.exceptions: Right-hand column of the exercise: stress is not word-final when the word ends in a postposition or enclitic (mã, kam, re, ri, bê): pur̲mã, mỳ̲kam, ngri̲re, te̲bê etc; unwritten epenthetic vowels after final consonants (pp. 80-81, 90: 'Com determinadas consoantes finais, principalmente [r], ocorre a pronúncia de uma vogal subsequente à consoante que não aparece na forma escrita') are outside the written tonic syllable. Vocabulary glosses "'ỳr logo/quase (quando for acentuado)" (p. 44 area) and "wa aquele.. (acentuado)" show some particles have accented vs unaccented uses.
new_statements.identity_note: Salanova 2001 describes Mebengokre as spoken by the Xikrin (Cateté) and Kayapó Mẽkrãgnõti, with data from Ikrô Kayapó, Nory Kayapó and Kangroti Apinayé; the stress remarks are stated for Mebengokre generally (one alternation cited as Xikrin dialect). Jefferson's grammar is SIL-Brasil material for Kayapó [txu]. The catalog record rests on Stout & Thomson's Txukahamãe (Mẽtyktire) Kayapó.

new_statements.quote: A vogal final destas palavras é tida como previsível por Stout e Thomson (op. cit., p. 162), mas a regra para a sua inserção é em todo caso mais complexa do que estas autoras mantêm: a vogal é uma cópia do núcleo da sílaba tônica (subjacentemente final), exceto quando esta última vogal é /a/ nos verbos e outras palavras predicativas, e, nos nomes, quando ela é /a/, /ç/ ou /√/. Nestes casos, a vogal epentética é o default /i/. Além desta predizibilidade e do fato de que praticamente só nestes casos temos temas superficialmente paroxítonos em Mebengokre, três fatos adicionais merecem atenção: [...] [p. 20:] Tais síncopes de vogal são amplamente atestadas em elementos que não têm acento próprio, como é o caso das partículas {ga} e {dZa}.
new_statements.translation: The final vowel of these words is taken to be predictable by Stout and Thomson (op. cit., p. 162), but the rule for its insertion is in any case more complex than these authors maintain: the vowel is a copy of the nucleus of the tonic syllable (underlyingly final), except when this last vowel is /a/ in verbs and other predicative words, and, in nouns, when it is /a/, /ɔ/ or /ʌ/ [the text layer's /ç/ and /√/ are legacy-font glyphs for ɔ and ʌ]. In these cases the epenthetic vowel is the default /i/. Besides this predictability and the fact that practically only in these cases do we have surface-paroxytone themes in Mebengokre, three additional facts deserve attention: ... [p. 20:] Such vowel syncopes are widely attested in elements that have no accent of their own, as is the case of the particles {ga} and {dZa}.
new_statements.citation: Salanova, Andrés Pablo (2001). A nasalidade me Mebengokre e Apinayé: o limite do vozeamento soante. Campinas: Univ. Universidade Estadual de Campinas. vii+93 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Stout & Thomson 1974: intensity normally on the last syllable of the word theme = fixed-dominant final): Salanova likewise places the tonic syllable stem-finally ('subjacentemente final') and adds (a) that apparent penultimate-stress words are final-stress stems plus a predictable epenthetic vowel after coda /r/, correcting Stout & Thomson's simpler epenthesis rule, and (b) that particles are unaccented. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section (the thesis is about nasality and voicing), but the author treats the tonic syllable of a Mebengokre theme as its underlyingly final syllable; words that surface as paroxytones do so practically only because a predictable epenthetic (echo or default /i/) vowel is added after a coda /r/ (e.g. ['pari] 'pé' < /par/), i.e. stress stays on the last lexical vowel; grammatical particles (pronouns {ga}, irrealis {dZa}, TAM markers, exclamations) have no accent of their own. Transcriptions throughout mark stress on the final stem syllable ([kç'rçrç] 'raso', [b√'¯o)ro)] 'embira', [pu gu'kRe)]).
new_statements.exceptions: surface penultimate stress only where a final epenthetic vowel follows coda /r/ (copy vowel, or default /i/ after /a/ in verbs and after /a ɔ ʌ/ in nouns); the epenthetic vowel drops before another vowel in the same phonological word; unstressed particles; author notes (p. 26 fn. 32) that few polysyllabic Mebengokre roots are non-compound, so statements about unstressed syllables are hard to make categorical
new_statements.identity_note: Salanova 2001 describes Mebengokre as spoken by the Xikrin (Cateté) and Kayapó Mẽkrãgnõti, with data from Ikrô Kayapó, Nory Kayapó and Kangroti Apinayé; the stress remarks are stated for Mebengokre generally (one alternation cited as Xikrin dialect). new_statements.translation: 5. STRESS. Stress is not predictable in phonological terms. Grammatically, it normally falls on the last syllable of the stem of the word. /pu'nu/ 'bad' /pu'nu-re/ 'a little bad (diminutive)'. [Table column headings:] 'Following a nasalized vowel at the end of the stressed syllable (word-final)' / 'Following an oral vowel at the end of the stressed syllable (word-final)' / 'Following an unstressed vowel (word-medial)'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records final stress (final stress = rightmost syllable). Stout & Thomson agree that stress is on the last syllable but specify the domain as the word stem (tema), with post-stem suffixes such as diminutive -re unstressed, and explicitly call stress phonologically unpredictable for that reason (morphologically conditioned final stress). Compatible with the catalog; adds the stem-domain condition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (intensidade) falls on the final syllable of the word stem (tema); it is stated to be not phonologically predictable because suffixal material such as the diminutive -re stays outside the stress domain (pu'nu 'bad' -> pu'nu-re 'baddish', stress does not shift). The allophone tables consistently equate the word-final syllable with the stressed syllable ('sílaba tônica (final de palavra)') and word-medial syllables with unstressed ones ('átona (média de palavra)'), and the transcriptions throughout mark stress on the last full syllable (a'kot, ika'mï, ku'pip; apparent initial-stress forms like ['tutU] 'pombo', ['tïrï] 'banana' involve the non-syllabic echo vowels of sec. 4.7, phonemically /tut/, /tïr/).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; note 2 states the analysis does not include units larger than the syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes/enclitics after the stem (example: diminutive -re) do not take stress, so stress can be word-penultimate on the surface; 'normalmente' signals the stem-final placement is the norm, without listing lexical exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Stout & Thomson describe the Txukahamãe (Txukarramãe, Mẽtyktire) group of Northern Kayapó (Mebêngôkre), data collected at Porori village, Parque Nacional do Xingu, 1965-1970; same language as the catalog's 'Kayapo' (kaya1330), a specific Xingu dialect group.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim on the page scan of the scan we hold, Stout & Thomson 1974:163 §5, suffix -řɛ as the compilers noted. (2) Deciding source is a 1974 SIL phonemic article; it is the classic source but we also HOLD the best modern description (Costa 2015 UnB PhD grammar, pp.45-46: primary stress 'com maior frequência' on the word-final syllable, exceptions = extrametrical suffixes like atenuativo -ɾɛ [puˈnuɾɛ] and echo-vowel forms — the same puˈnu / puˈnu-ɾɛ pair as Stout & Thomson) and I downloaded Salanova & Nikulin 2020:69 ('o acento em Mẽbêngôkre recai na última sílaba, com raríssimas exceções'; unstressed enclitic =re, post-tonic epenthetic vowels, falling diphthongs). Three independent descriptions (1974 Txukahamãe, 2015 Xikrín, 2020 pan-dialectal) agree: regular final stress on the stem/lexical word, weight-blind, with a closed set of unstressed post-stem elements. sources.quote: A vogal final destas palavras é tida como previsível por Stout e Thomson (op. cit., p. 162), mas a regra para a sua inserção é em todo caso mais complexa do que estas autoras mantêm: a vogal é uma cópia do núcleo da sílaba tônica (subjacentemente final), exceto quando esta última vogal é /a/ nos verbos e outras palavras predicativas, e, nos nomes, quando ela é /a/, /ç/ ou /√/. Nestes casos, a vogal epentética é o default /i/. Além desta predizibilidade e do fato de que praticamente só nestes casos temos temas superficialmente paroxítonos em Mebengokre, três fatos adicionais merecem atenção: [...] [p. 20:] Tais síncopes de vogal são amplamente atestadas em elementos que não têm acento próprio, como é o caso das partículas {ga} e {dZa}.

sources.note: Compatible with the catalog record (Stout & Thomson 1974: intensity normally on the last syllable of the word theme = fixed-dominant final): Salanova likewise places the tonic syllable stem-finally ('subjacentemente final') and adds (a) that apparent penultimate-stress words are final-stress stems plus a predictable epenthetic vowel after coda /r/, correcting Stout & Thomson's simpler epenthesis rule, and (b) that particles are unaccented. No contradiction.

sources.note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records final stress (final stress = rightmost syllable). Stout & Thomson agree that stress is on the last syllable but specify the domain as the word stem (tema), with post-stem suffixes such as diminutive -re unstressed, and explicitly call stress phonologically unpredictable for that reason (morphologically conditioned final stress). Compatible with the catalog; adds the stem-domain condition.

sources.citation: Salanova, Andrés Pablo & Andrey Nikulin. 2020. A história que conta o léxico Mẽbêngôkre. Revista de Letras Norte@mentos 13(33): 52-106 (Dossiê: Para a década das línguas indígenas). Open PDF via Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú.
sources.quote: 'Finalmente, o acento em Mẽbêngôkre recai na última sílaba, com raríssimas exceções.' Exceptions listed: (i) obligatory vowel epenthesis after underlying final /ɾ/ creates a few post-tonic syllables; (ii) words ending in falling diphthongs surface with stress on the penultimate vowel (ngija [ˈŋija], kruwa [ˈkɾuwa]); (iii) unstressed enclitics, notably diminutive =re (vs. tonic augmentative -ti), yield non-final stress in the phonological word. Fn.12: compounds keep secondary stress on each subordinate stem, primary on the last ([ˌɾɔmˈnɔ] 'lanterna').
